overview.what: A two-servo arm driven by an ESP32 that finds the ISS's position online, works out where it is in your sky and points a pointer at it.
overview.why: It adds motors, Wi-Fi and real maths to your skills. You will turn a position in space into two angles, then into movement.
overview.spaceRelevance: Ground stations point dishes at satellites in exactly this way, using a TLE and two angles. Your arm is a toy version of that real job.
overview.finalOutput: A pan and tilt arm that follows the ISS around the sky, plus code and a short video.
overview.estimatedTime: 3 to 4 weeks at 3 to 4 hours a week

roadmap.title: Meet your target
roadmap.learn: How big, how high and how fast the ISS is.
roadmap.explain: The International Space Station is about the size of a football pitch. It orbits roughly 420 km above you at about 27,600 km/h, so it circles Earth once in around 93 minutes. That is 15 or 16 laps a day. From the ground it looks like a bright, fast star that crosses the sky in a few minutes. Your arm will have to keep up with it.
roadmap.implement: Open the live ISS position at wheretheiss.at. Note its altitude and speed, then compare them with the numbers here.
roadmap.outcome: You know what you are pointing at.

figure.alt: The International Space Station seen from a departing shuttle, with gold-coloured modules and dark solar panels against blue ocean and white cloud.
figure.caption: The ISS from the Space Shuttle in 2005. Its solar panels face the Sun, and the whole station flies at about 7.7 km each second.

resources.label: Where is the ISS right now?

roadmap.title: Why satellites stay up
roadmap.learn: The one idea behind every orbit.
roadmap.explain: An orbit is falling that never lands. The ISS is pulled towards Earth all the time, but it also moves sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it as quickly as it falls. Gravity does not switch off up there, and it is still almost 90 percent as strong as at the surface. Astronauts float because they are falling with the station, not because gravity is missing.
roadmap.implement: Watch the video. Then explain, in two sentences to a friend, why the ISS does not fall down.
roadmap.outcome: You can explain what an orbit is.

figure.title: How Do Satellites Get & Stay in Orbit?
figure.caption: Four minutes on the sideways-speed idea, which is the base for the rest of this project.

roadmap.title: Azimuth and elevation
roadmap.learn: The two angles that say where to look in the sky.
roadmap.explain: To point at something you need two numbers. Azimuth is the compass direction, measured clockwise from north: 0 is north, 90 is east, 180 is south and 270 is west. Elevation is how high above the horizon, from 0 at the horizon to 90 straight up. The ISS is only visible when its elevation is above 0. These two angles will become the angles of your two servos.
roadmap.implement: Stand outside with a phone compass. Point at a tree and write down its azimuth, and guess its elevation. Then check the picture to be sure you can read both angles.
roadmap.outcome: You can describe any point in the sky with two numbers.

figure.alt: Left: a compass seen from above with an arrow at 60 degrees from north. Right: a side view with a dashed line rising 35 degrees from the horizon to the ISS.
figure.caption: Azimuth goes around the compass. Elevation goes up from the horizon. Together they point anywhere.

roadmap.title: TLEs: an orbit in two lines
roadmap.learn: How a few numbers describe where a satellite will be.
roadmap.explain: A TLE, or two-line element set, is two lines of numbers that describe one satellite's orbit. The ISS entry includes its tilt (about 51.6 degrees) and how many laps it makes per day (about 15.5). Feed a TLE into a standard maths model called SGP4 and you get the satellite's position at any time. Drag from air, and now and then a thruster burn, change the orbit, so a TLE goes stale after a few days. Get a new one often.
roadmap.implement: Open the CelesTrak page for the ISS in the resources. Find the line starting with 2 and pick out the tilt, which is the first number after 25544.
roadmap.outcome: You know what a TLE holds and why it needs refreshing.

figure.alt: Left: Earth with the ISS orbit drawn as a tilted ellipse, tilted 51.6 degrees from the equator. Right: a TLE feeds orbit maths, which gives the position right now.
figure.caption: The orbit is a fixed tilted ring and the Earth turns beneath it. That is why the ISS passes over different places each lap.

roadmap.title: Predict a pass with Python
roadmap.learn: How to use a TLE to know when the ISS will be overhead.
roadmap.explain: Python can do the SGP4 maths for you with a library called Skyfield. You give it a TLE and your latitude and longitude, and it finds each time the ISS rises over a minimum height, reaches its highest point and sets. Times come out in UTC. India is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of UTC, so add that to get local time. Use 10 degrees as the cut-off, because objects near the horizon are hidden by trees and buildings.
roadmap.implement: Install Skyfield with pip install skyfield. Change the latitude and longitude to your own, run this and note the next pass in local time.
roadmap.outcome: You have a list of the next ISS passes over your college.

figure.code:
import urllib.request
from skyfield.api import EarthSatellite, load, wgs84   # pip install skyfield

url = "https://celestrak.org/NORAD/elements/gp.php?CATNR=25544&FORMAT=TLE"
name, line1, line2 = urllib.request.urlopen(url).read().decode().splitlines()

ts = load.timescale()
iss = EarthSatellite(line1, line2, name.strip(), ts)
you = wgs84.latlon(28.61, 77.21)          # your latitude and longitude

start = ts.now()
times, events = iss.find_events(you, start, start + 1, altitude_degrees=10)
for t, e in zip(times, events):           # 0 = rises, 1 = highest, 2 = sets
    print(t.utc_strftime("%d %b %H:%M UTC"), ["rises", "highest", "sets"][e])
figure.caption: Prints when the ISS rises, peaks and sets over your location in the next 24 hours. It needs an internet connection to fetch the TLE.

roadmap.title: Work out the angles yourself
roadmap.learn: How to turn a latitude and longitude into azimuth and elevation.
roadmap.explain: A live position service gives latitude, longitude and height. You need to turn that into the two angles. Place you and the ISS as points in 3D, subtract them to get the arrow from you to the ISS, then split that arrow into east, north and up. Azimuth is the angle of the east and north parts, and elevation is the angle of the up part. This code does it with plain maths. Skyfield gives the same answer to within a tenth of a degree.
roadmap.implement: Run the code. An ISS at latitude 0, longitude 5, 420 km high, seen from 0, 0, should give azimuth 90 and elevation 33.7. Change the numbers and sanity check each result.
roadmap.outcome: Your own function turns a position into pointing angles.

figure.code:
import math
R = 6371.0                         # Earth's radius, km

def xyz(lat, lon, r):              # a point above Earth as x, y, z in km
    la, lo = math.radians(lat), math.radians(lon)
    return (r*math.cos(la)*math.cos(lo), r*math.cos(la)*math.sin(lo), r*math.sin(la))

def az_el(lat, lon, iss_lat, iss_lon, iss_km):
    me, iss = xyz(lat, lon, R), xyz(iss_lat, iss_lon, R + iss_km)
    dx, dy, dz = (iss[i] - me[i] for i in range(3))     # arrow from you to the ISS
    a, b = math.radians(lat), math.radians(lon)
    flat = math.cos(b)*dx + math.sin(b)*dy
    east = -math.sin(b)*dx + math.cos(b)*dy
    north = -math.sin(a)*flat + math.cos(a)*dz
    up = math.cos(a)*flat + math.sin(a)*dz
    az = math.degrees(math.atan2(east, north)) % 360
    return az, math.degrees(math.atan2(up, math.hypot(east, north)))

print(az_el(0, 0, 0, 5, 420))      # 90.0 and 33.7: east, and well up
figure.caption: The same maths you will later put on the ESP32. The Earth is treated as a sphere, which is accurate enough to aim a plastic arm.

roadmap.title: How a servo works
roadmap.learn: What a hobby servo does and how it is told where to turn.
roadmap.explain: A servo is a small motor with a gear train and a sensor inside, so it knows its own angle. You tell it where to go with a signal that repeats 50 times a second. The width of each pulse sets the angle, and the servo turns until it gets there and then holds on. An SG90 turns about 180 degrees. That is enough for the arm, as the next steps show.
roadmap.implement: Watch the video. In Wokwi build a circuit with an ESP32 and one servo on GPIO 18. Sweep it from 0 to 180 with a for loop and write(angle).
roadmap.outcome: A virtual servo sweeps back and forth.

figure.title: What is a Servo Motor and What Does It Do?
figure.caption: A clear three minute look inside a servo and how its control signal works.

roadmap.title: Cover the whole sky with two servos
roadmap.learn: How to point anywhere with parts that turn only 180 degrees.
roadmap.explain: One servo turns the arm around, called pan, and a second tilts it up. A servo turns only 180 degrees, so pan alone covers half the compass. The trick is to let the tilt servo go past vertical. For a target in the other half, turn the pan servo to azimuth minus 180 and tilt 180 minus the elevation. The arm leans over the top and ends up pointing at the right place. Two small servos can now reach the whole sky.
roadmap.implement: Add a second servo on GPIO 19 in Wokwi. Run this code. It should send the arm to the west, 30 degrees up, which means pan 90 and tilt 150.
roadmap.outcome: Two servos can aim at any azimuth and elevation.

figure.caption: Compile and test in Wokwi. After you build the arm, adjust the angles so that pan 0 really points north.

roadmap.title: Build the arm
roadmap.learn: How to mount two servos so they pan and tilt.
roadmap.explain: Glue or screw the pan servo upright to a flat base so its horn spins horizontally. Fix the tilt servo to that horn, and put a long thin pointer, such as a straw or a skewer, on the tilt servo's horn. Add a small weight or tape at the base so it does not tip. Cardboard, craft sticks and hot glue are enough. A 3D-printed bracket is a bonus, not a need.
roadmap.implement: Build the arm. Centre both servos at 90 before you glue the horns, so that the pointer stands straight up. Mark north on the base with tape.
roadmap.outcome: A working pan and tilt arm that can point at a wall.

figure.caption: An SG90 micro servo. The wires are brown for ground, red for power and orange for the signal.

roadmap.title: Wire it and power it safely
roadmap.learn: How to power servos without crashing the ESP32.
roadmap.explain: Servos pull sudden bursts of current, up to several hundred milliamps each when they start or get stuck. Powering them from the ESP32's own supply can make the board reset. Give the servos their own 5 volt supply, such as a USB power bank with a breakout board. Then join the grounds. A signal needs a shared zero volt reference, or the servo sees noise. Never wire a servo's power to a GPIO pin.
roadmap.implement: Wire the arm as shown. Connect the ground of the supply to an ESP32 GND pin. Add a 470 microfarad capacitor across the supply if the board still resets.
roadmap.outcome: The servos run from their own supply and the ESP32 stays steady.

figure.alt: Wiring diagram: ESP32 GPIO 18 goes to the pan servo signal and GPIO 19 to the tilt servo signal. A 5 volt power bank feeds both servos, and its ground joins the ESP32 ground.
figure.caption: The signal wires come from the ESP32. The power comes from the power bank. Only the ground is shared.

roadmap.title: Fetch the live ISS position
roadmap.learn: How the ESP32 asks the internet where the ISS is.
roadmap.explain: The ESP32 joins Wi-Fi and sends a web request, like a browser would. The service wheretheiss.at answers with JSON that includes latitude, longitude and altitude. ArduinoJson turns the text into numbers. setInsecure() skips checking the site's certificate, which is acceptable for a public data feed and would be wrong for anything with a password. In Wokwi, the network named Wokwi-GUEST is free and has internet.
roadmap.implement: Install ArduinoJson (version 7). Add this function, join Wokwi-GUEST in setup and print the latitude and longitude. Compare them with the website.
roadmap.outcome: Your ESP32 prints the ISS position every few seconds.

figure.caption: Fetches latitude, longitude and height. If the service is ever down, getIss returns false and the arm simply stays where it is.

roadmap.title: Aim at the ISS
roadmap.learn: How to put the pieces together.
roadmap.explain: The C++ function azEl() is your Python maths ported across. It takes your latitude and longitude, and the ISS position, and gives azimuth and elevation. When the elevation is below 0 the ISS is on the other side of Earth, so the arm stays where it is. The next step calls it in a loop that waits five seconds between requests.
roadmap.implement: Paste azEl above setup and set MY_LAT and MY_LON. Print its result for the live position and compare it with Skyfield or N2YO at the same moment.
roadmap.outcome: The simulated arm follows the ISS around your sky.

figure.caption: azEl() in C++. Set const float MY_LAT and MY_LON to your own place, with north and east positive.

roadmap.title: Calibrate and test outside
roadmap.learn: How to make the arm point at the real ISS.
roadmap.explain: Wokwi cannot tell you if your arm really points north. Put the arm on a flat surface. Use a phone compass to turn the base until pan 0 faces true north, and mark it. Use the phone's level to check that tilt 90 is vertical. Then run the loop at a time when the ISS is high in your sky, ideally just after dusk. Hold a phone sky map beside the arm and compare. Expect an error of a few degrees.
roadmap.implement: Add the loop below, flash the real board and take the arm outside for a visible pass. Adjust offsets in point() until the pointer lines up, then ask a friend to take a photo.
roadmap.outcome: The arm points at the real ISS to within a few degrees.

figure.caption: The main loop. It fetches the position, finds the angles, moves the arm and waits.

roadmap.title: Publish your pointer
roadmap.learn: How to share a physical project.
roadmap.explain: A hardware project needs more than code. Add the wiring picture, the code, a photo or short video of the arm moving and a note on what you would improve. Mention the limits too: sphere maths, a few degrees of error and a stale clock if your Wi-Fi drops. A reader can then trust your results and rebuild your arm.
roadmap.implement: Push the code, wiring picture, a README and a short video of the arm tracking to GitHub.
roadmap.outcome: The pointer is documented and published.
